claims.text: Under separation and sufficiency, either the outcome and score are jointly independent of the sensitive attribute, or an event in the joint distribution has probability zero.
Achieving balance for both negative and positive classes alongside within-group calibration requires either equal base rates across protected groups or perfect prediction accuracy.
A scoring function exhibiting both separation and demographic parity implies either equal base rates across groups or zero predictive utility.
A scoring function exhibiting both sufficiency and demographic parity implies equal base rates across protected groups.
Decision rules that maximize utility under a demographic parity constraint generally require using sensitive attributes during both probability estimation and threshold selection.
Single-threshold decision rules maximize expected utility when scores accurately estimate outcome probabilities and utilities satisfy separate, symmetric, and simultaneous evaluation assumptions.
Mathematical definitions of algorithmic fairness evaluated solely on decision-subject populations fail to account for bias in the mechanisms that govern population entry.

evidence.description: The authors state that Barocas et al. and Wasserman show that under separation (S ⊥ A | Y) and sufficiency (Y ⊥ A | S), either (Y,S) ⊥ A or an event in the joint distribution has probability zero.
Kleinberg et al. showed that satisfying balance for the negative class, balance for the positive class, and calibration within groups requires either equal base rates (Y ⊥ A) or perfect prediction.
Barocas et al. showed that when Y is binary and the scoring function exhibits separation and demographic parity, there must be either equal base rates or a useless predictor (Y ⊥ S).
Barocas et al. showed that if a model satisfies sufficiency and demographic parity, then there must be equal base rates: Y ⊥ A.

Corbett-Davies et al. and Lipton et al. note that a decision rule maximizing utility under a demographic parity constraint generally uses sensitive variables both in estimating conditional probabilities and determining thresholds.

The paper references utility maximization results showing single-threshold optimality when scores approximate conditional probabilities and utility functions satisfy separate, symmetric, and simultaneous assumptions.

The paper notes that a model satisfying fairness criteria evaluated only on the population to which it is applied may overlook unfairness in the selection mechanism that brought individuals into that population.

methodologies.name: Systematic Literature Taxonomy and Survey of Algorithmic Fairness Definitions
methodologies.description: Categorizes choices, assumptions, and mathematical definitions of fairness in machine learning, contrasting oblivious metrics with metric-based and causal frameworks.
conditions: Binary decision-making settings based on binary outcome predictions
Application to pretrial risk assessment and loan default prediction scenarios

limitations.text: Oblivious fairness metrics evaluate distributions of observed features, outcomes, scores, and decisions without referencing external social context or structural inequalities.
Implementing metric fairness in practice is difficult due to the challenge of explicitly defining distance metrics over high-dimensional feature spaces.
Causal fairness definitions require making unverifiable assumptions about counterfactuals or requiring direct access to internal model mechanisms.
The paper focuses primarily on summarizing and cataloguing existing formal definitions without advancing new axiomatic mathematical definitions of fairness.

future_work.text: Develop causal reasoning frameworks to design earlier structural interventions prior to decision-making rather than solely defining fairness constraints at decision time.
Construct expanded decision models and utility functions that account for interference, heterogeneous treatment effects, and serial or temporal dynamic impacts.
